judgments.catchwords: 1. Two Siblings and Three Estates. 2. The contesting parties, as the sole surviving members of their immediate family, are entangled in a protracted and bitter dispute over the estates left behind by their late parents and brother. 3. The Plaintiff and the Defendant had initially elected to regulate the distribution of the estates through a Deed of Settlement executed between them. One might have expected this to bring finality to the matter. Alas, the passage of time, some ten years or so, has done little to quell their discord. Despite having taken what appeared to be a significant step towards resolving their differences, disagreements continued to simmer. Grievances deepened, trust eroded, and the relationship between the siblings deteriorated further. Eventually, the Plaintiff commenced the present suit against the Defendant, to which the Defendant responded with a counterclaim of his own. 7. At its core, the principal question is whether the Deed of Settlement dated 21 December 2018 constitutes a valid and binding agreement between the parties or whether, for the reasons advanced by the Defendant, it is liable to be declared void ab initio or otherwise unenforceable. 8. If the Deed of Settlement is found to be valid and binding, the Court must then determine whether the Defendant acted in breach of its terms, whether he is estopped from challenging its validity after having accepted benefits under the settlement, and whether the Plaintiff is entitled to the reliefs claimed. 9. The Court must also consider the Defendant's contention that the validity of the Deed of Settlement cannot be determined without reference to the applicable principles of Syariah law, including whether the Deed complies with the relevant requirements of Islamic law and the extent, if any, to which the Power of Attorney dated 5 November 2011 bears upon the issues in dispute.

judgments.catchwords: CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Appeal — Sentence — Appellate interference — Principles of interference — Whether sentence was wrong in principle or manifestly excessive — Priority of public interest over personal mitigation in serious offences — Whether plea of guilty entitles an accused to an automatic reduction in sentence — Plea of guilty not a strong mitigating factor where offence is grave and threatens public safety PENAL CODE: s 435 — Mischief by fire — Penal Code (Amendment) Act 2014 — Sentence of maximum penalty from seven to fourteen years as indicator of gravity On 16.10.2024, at approximately 2.00 a.m., a fire broke out at the Complainant's house located at No. 121, FELDA Kesumba Jengka 9, Bandar Jengka, Pahang. The Complainant and her child managed to extinguish the fire before lodging a police report, recorded as Bandar Jengka Report No. 2606/2024. On the following day, the Appellant telephoned the Complainant's son, Mohamad Riduan bin Zulkapli, and admitted responsibility for the incident, stating that there was no need to look for anyone else. The conversation was recorded by the Complainant's daughter, Nor Surena binti Zulkapli. Subsequently, on 20.10.2024, the Appellant was arrested in connection with the incident pursuant to Bandar Jengka Report No. 2650/2024. A preliminary report issued by the Fire and Rescue Department on 23.10.2024 concluded that the fire was incendiary in nature, following which the Appellant was charged with an offence under Section 435 of the Penal Code. On 16.07.2025, the Appellant pleaded guilty to the charge before the learned Sessions Court Judge and, being unrepresented, was sentenced to five (5) years' imprisonment commencing from 16.07.2025 and a fine of RM10,000.00, in default of one (1) year's imprisonment.

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya v MOHD REDWAN BIN HUSAIN
judgments.catchwords: CRIMINAL LAW: Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 — Section 39B(1)(a) — Trafficking in dangerous drugs — Methamphetamine — Net weight 51.83 grams — Elements of the offence — Identity and weight of drug — Actual custody, control, and possession — Act of trafficking — Ingredients to be established at close of prosecution case. EVIDENCE: Expert evidence — Chemist report — Acceptance on "face value" — Munusamy v. PP distinguished — Rejection of "face value" doctrine where foundational scientific premises challenged — Borderline weight — Electronic weighing scale — Lack of calibration certificate — Absence of proof of calibration at material time — Unresolved margin of error — Statutory presumption under s. 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 disentitled. EVIDENCE: Representative sampling — Section 37(j) of Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 — Statutorily defective sampling methodology — Chemist analyzing only 0.23% (175mg) of net bulk (74.80g) — Statistical inadequacy — Adequacy of sample a question of fact for the court, not the expert — Finding in the lower degree where doubt exists on capital threshold — PP v. Samundee Devan Muthu Kerishnan applied — Homogenization process — Homogenized bulk remainder (P19) failing to fit back into original seized packets (P16–P18) — Unexplained physical volume discrepancy — Rejection of unevidenced submission from the bar on "volume expansion". EVIDENCE: Chain of custody — Requisition form (Borang Pol 31) prepared but not produced in court — Non-receipt by chemist of seized outer container (green plastic bag P21) — Interruption in chain of custody and store registration. EVIDENCE: Documentary and physical evidence — "Silent evidence" — Conflicting crime scene photographs and sketch plans — Locus in quo depicted as T-junction in prosecution exhibits (P8, P10) versus straight road in admitted defence exhibit (D24) — Unrecorded additions made to sketch plan long after arrest — Interjection on record by arresting officer that photos shown were "not the same" — Prosecution leading two irreconcilable narratives — Benefit of doubt given to accused — Farisha Azwa Abdullah, PP v. Lee Eng Kooi, and PP v. Woon Shi Hong applied. CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Search and seizure — Search list (Borang Bongkar P6) compiled away from locus in quo at police station/office — Non-compliance with Section 64 of Criminal Procedure Code — Loss of contemporaneous character under Sections 91 and 92 of Evidence Act 1950 — PP v. Sulaiman Pawanteh and PP v. Muhammad Fitri Saad applied. CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Arrest and investigation — Simultaneous arrest of third party (Mohd Uzair) at same time and location — Failure of prosecution to exclude third-party access or investigate nexus to seized contraband — Unshifting burden of proof on prosecution — Legentheraj Asogan v. PP applied. EVIDENCE: Fingerprint evidence — Absence of fingerprints on drug wrappings — Primary factual admission in prosecution's case-in-chief via written witness statement (PSSP3) — Failure to cross-examine on admitted fact legally redundant — Rejection of speculative submissions on "sweat" and "bag handles" — Distinguishing PP v. Mansor Md Rashid where sole eyewitness narrative is compromised. STATUTORY PRESUMPTIONS: Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 — Section 37(da)(xvi) — Presumption of trafficking — Statutory gateways of threshold weight and actual possession unproven — Prohibition against double presumptions under s. 37(d) and s. 37(da) — Sathya Vello v. PP applied. CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Trial — Close of prosecution case — Prima facie case — Section 180 of Criminal Procedure Code — Maximum evaluation of evidence — Cumulative "snowball effect" of multiple procedural, factual, and scientific flaws — Prosecution narrative fundamentally fractured — Order of acquittal and discharge without calling for defence — PP v. Shaharudin Musa applied.

judgments.title: VIJIYAN RAO A/L SUBRAMANIAM v Pendakwa Raya
judgments.catchwords: Criminal appeals – against conviction and sentences under s. 13(a) of the Anti-Trafficking in Persons and Anti-Smuggling of Migrants Act 2007, s. 326 of the Penal Code and s. 55B of the Immigration Act Non-compliance of s. 51A of the CPC - while s. 51A(c) of the CPC imposes a statutory obligation on the prosecution to deliver a written statement of facts favourable to the defence, non-compliance therewith does not automatically render the entire trial null and void - the word 'shall' in subsection (1) of s. 51A of the CPC means directory - non-compliance with s. 51A of the CPC would not statutorily prevent the prosecution from tendering the documents which were not delivered to the accused person before trial as evidence in the course of the trial - it is only procedural and not evidential. Common intention under s. 34 of the PC - direct evidence of a pre-arranged plan is not a prerequisite - common intention may be readily inferred from the surrounding circumstantial evidence, including the acts, conduct, and behaviour of the accused parties both preceding and during the commission of the offence.

judgments.title: G VENTURE ADVISORY SDN BHD v Noor Jeehan Binti Adam
judgments.catchwords: Lampiran 15 adalah permohonan daripada pihak Penghutang Penghakiman (“JD”) untuk mengenepikan Notis Kebankrapan yang difailkan oleh pihak Pemiutang Penghakiman (“JC”) bertarikh 24/10/2025 dan Perintah Penyampaian Ganti bertarikh 10/12/2025. 1. Mahkamah ini berpendapat bahawa cubaan serahan secara kediri telah dibuat dengan sempurna di alamat yang telah dinyatakan di Perjanjian yang menjadi asas kepada tindakan kebankrapan ini dan oleh itu, perintah penyampaian ganti tersebut adalah sah. Mahkamah bersetuju dengan hujahan pihak JC bahawa pendedahan tersebut adalah dibuat oleh pihak JD sendiri selepas serahan secara penyampaian ganti telah disempurnakan. 2. Mahkamah ini bersetuju dengan pihak JC bahawa kesilapan nama dalam sistem e-filing bukanlah satu kesilapan yang memprejudiskan pihak JD dan tidak membatalkan Notis Kebankrapan. 3. Seterusnya, mahkamah bersetuju dengan hujahan pihak JD bahawa isu berkaitan forum non conveniens adalah relevan untuk dipertimbangkan memandangkan JD kini menetap di Melaka. Namun begitu, ia bukanlah satu isu yang membatalkan terus Notis Kebankrapan ini. 4. Selain itu, undang-undang adalah mantap bahawa mahkamah kebankrapan tidak boleh bertindak membelakangkan perintah yang telah diperolehi di mahkamah asal. Mahkamah kebankrapan ini bukanlah platform yang sesuai untuk menentukan kesahihan Pinjaman Jaminan tersebut. 5. Akhir sekali, mahkamah ini berpendapat bahawa isu berkaitan set off penghakiman terhadap pihak ketiga bukanlah satu alasan yang relevan untuk dipertimbangkan. Oleh itu, Lampiran 15 ditolak dengan perintah terhadap kos sebanyak RM500.00 sahaja.
